GM Cares visitThursday, Oct. 22, 2026 · Columbia Ridge Elementary, Ephrata

Ephrata built a robot, then took Tiger Pride to the national stage.

Ridge Robotics is the FIRST LEGO League team from Columbia Ridge Elementary. Last season nine fourth-graders won Engineering Excellence at the Eastern Washington State Championship, were drawn as one of ten Washington teams for a national open, and set a personal-best 180 points in New Jersey.6 9 13 On October 22, GM Cares comes to say thank you, and to help this year's team go further.

The celebration

A season worth a cake

How the season unfolded

  1. Fall 2025

    UNEARTHED kickoff

    The archaeology-themed FIRST LEGO League season. Ridge Robotics joined teams from Grant Elementary, Parkway Intermediate and Ephrata Middle School in the district's robotics lineup.12 21

  2. December 6, 2025

    Qualifier, Spokane · Core Values Award

    Recognized for exemplifying FLL's six core values: Discovery, Innovation, Impact, Inclusion, Teamwork and Fun. Advanced to state.4 5

  3. January 24, 2026

    Eastern Washington State Championship · Engineering Excellence

    Three robot rounds plus a judged presentation. The team built a sensor that let their robot tell water from electrolytes by color, an idea the students said they were proudest of.6 7 8

  4. February 2026

    Drawn for the national open

    FIRST Washington's lottery sent four Washington teams to New Jersey, Ridge Robotics among them. Rep. Dan Newhouse wrote to commend the students' "skill, teamwork, and sportsmanship."9 12

  5. February 23, 2026

    School Board approves the trip

    Out-of-state travel, lodging and participation approved for students and coaches.7 8

  6. June 6–7, 2026

    American Robotics Open Championship, Madison, NJ

    Personal-best 180 points, National Anthem at opening ceremonies, and a 30-minute judging session with no coaches or parents in the room, where they presented a hydration vest designed to keep archaeologists safe on dig sites.13 14

They've moved up. The torch has not.

Columbia Ridge serves kindergarten through fourth grade, so every member of last year's team was a fourth-grader.3 6 This fall they started at Parkway Intermediate, Ephrata's grade 5–6 school, which runs its own LEGO Robotics program.19 20 That means the 2026–27 Ridge Robotics team is a brand-new group of Tigers, picking up the torch for the BIOGLOW season with a trophy case to live up to and a path they can now see all the way to a national stage.

What makes this program different

They are young. Every Ridge Robotics athlete competes up an age bracket, often against middle schoolers.6 3 They are consistent. This is not a one-season story: the 2024–25 team took a shark-shaped reef-cleaning capsule to the Pasco qualifier in the SUBMERGED season, and the 2025–26 team went to nationals.21 13 And they are generous. Judges at the qualifier and at state honored the team for how they treated each other and their competitors.5 12 The program's own words: students "proudly representing the community with Tiger Pride."1

This season · 2026–27

BIOGLOW: ideas for the Ridge Robotics playbook

The FIRST CANOPY season launched August 4, 2026. The FIRST LEGO League challenge is BIOGLOW, built around biodiversity: how technology, creativity and field research help us understand and protect living things.22 23 Challenge teams run a SPIKE Prime robot through two-and-a-half-minute matches and present an Innovation Project to judges.23 22 Grant County happens to be a biodiversity goldmine. A few starting points, offered as ideas, not assignments.

Innovation Project · local hook

Soap Lake literally glows

Five miles up the road, Soap Lake is one of the world's few meromictic lakes, with a mineral-rich bottom layer that hosts unusual microbial life. A team that studies what lives in Soap Lake, Moses Lake or the Potholes, and designs a way to protect or monitor it, is telling a BIOGLOW story no other team in the country can tell. Ask the Soap Lake Conservancy or WSU Extension for a guest expert.

Innovation Project

Pollinators for the orchards

Apples and cherries around Ephrata depend on bees. Ideas: a bee-hotel with a temperature sensor, a bloom-timing alert for growers, or a kid-built pollinator strip plan for the school grounds.

Innovation Project

Salmon and the Columbia

Fish passage, water temperature and side-channel habitat. A model of a smart fish counter or a cooling shade structure makes a great judging prop.

Innovation Project

Sage grouse and shrub-steppe

Beezley Hills is right above town. A trail camera triggered only by motion of a certain size, or a seed-planting robot for sagebrush restoration.

Innovation Project

Bats, the quiet pest control

Bats eat orchard pests every night. A bat-house with a sound logger shows how biodiversity pays farmers back.

Robot Game · what Engineering Excellence judges look for

Win on consistency, not ambition

  • Pick the missions you can complete three out of three times. A reliable 200 beats an occasional 300.
  • Group missions by mat zone into "runs," and design one quick-change attachment per run. Time the swaps; they are part of the 2:30.
  • Square the robot against walls and use gyro turns, so every run starts from the same place. Last year's color sensor trick was this kind of thinking.6 7
  • Keep an engineering notebook: what you tried, what broke, what you changed. Judges read it. It is how Engineering Excellence gets awarded.
  • Rehearse the judging room without adults, exactly like New Jersey. The team already knows how.13 14
Core Values · the Tiger way

Keep doing the thing judges keep noticing

Two awards in one season were for how the team treats people.5 12 Bring a small gift or a cheer for the team at the next table. Help a team whose robot broke. Write it down afterward: judges ask for examples.

How a car sees the road

A self-driving system fuses cameras, radar and lidar the same way a FLL robot fuses color, distance and gyro sensors. Bob will demo the idea with the team's own robot, and the team can ask him anything about how GM builds and tests the AI behind a car.

How to help

Get this team back to the national stage

A trip like New Jersey costs real money: airfare for nine students and their coaches, lodging, registration and meals. The School Board can approve travel, but the community pays for it. Here is what the team needs, and how GM people in particular can multiply their help.

Volunteer

  • Practice-night mentorAn hour a week helping with code, attachments or the Innovation Project. No robotics background required; engineers, farmers, nurses and accountants all make great mentors.
  • Build a practice tableA 4×8 sheet of plywood and 2×4 rails, built to the official FLL table spec, gives the team a second place to practice.
  • Judge or referee a FIRST Washington eventEvents run on volunteers. Sign up at firstwa.org; it is a full, fun Saturday.25 16
  • Guest expertBiologists, orchardists, fisheries staff, beekeepers: a 20-minute visit gives the Innovation Project real sources to cite.
  • Travel-day chaperone or driverQualifiers in Spokane or Wapato mean early mornings and long days.

Contribute

  • Travel fundGifts to the Ridge Robotics ASB club are handled through Columbia Ridge Elementary and the Ephrata School District; call the school office to designate a gift.1 2 Note that GM's own Community Impact Grants fund STEM nonprofits but exclude robotics teams directly, so the school and FIRST Washington are the right channels.36 33
  • Team gear and snacksMatching shirts, a team banner, competition-day lunches.
  • GM employees: Dollars for DoersAfter 50 volunteer hours with one eligible nonprofit in a calendar year, GM grants that organization a Dollars for Doers award ($500 per Double the Donation's current listing; GM's own published guidelines and earlier announcements say $200). A team event totaling 50 hours also qualifies. Log hours through the GM Cares portal.33 34 35
  • GM employees: matching giftsGM matches employee donations made through the GM Cares giving portal; questions go to gmcares [at] gm.com.33 36
  • Anyone: a FIRST Washington donationFIRST Washington, the nonprofit that runs every qualifier and state event, accepts donations at firstwa.org.

Winning ways

How GM shows up for robotics, kids and the road ahead

GM Cares is not a slogan. It is a grassroots employee program that has been showing up in gyms and classrooms since 2011, and it sits on top of a company that helped found FIRST itself.

1.3M+ hours

GM Cares, by GM employees

Since 2011, GM employees have contributed more than 1.3 million volunteer hours and more than $16.3 million in direct donations to nonprofits through GM Cares, the company's global employee giving program.28 29 It grew out of teamGM Cares, a volunteer-led, company-wide employee initiative; in 2017 alone more than 18,000 GM employees logged 161,000 volunteer hours.30 31 32

Founding sponsor

GM and FIRST

GM is a Founding Sponsor of FIRST and sponsors or supports hundreds of teams; employees coach and mentor children ages 6 to 18 across all FIRST programs, including FIRST LEGO League.37 38 GM directly sponsors dozens of teams each season, supports hundreds more, and has reached more than 10,000 students through FIRST.38 39

1 billion

Hands-free miles on Super Cruise

GM customers have driven a billion hands-free miles on Super Cruise, across nearly 750,000 vehicles and 23 models, generating the real-world data that trains GM's AI models.40 41 It is the same loop a FLL team runs: drive, measure, fix, drive again.

2028

From hands-off to eyes-off

GM plans to launch eyes-off driving on highways starting with the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028, built on a new centralized computing architecture that scales from Cadillac to Chevrolet.42 47 CEO Mary Barra said in October 2026 the program remains on track.45 46

5M miles

What Cruise taught GM

Cruise logged more than 5 million fully driverless miles in some of the most complex cities in the country.42 44 GM wound down the robotaxi business in December 2024 and folded that work into autonomy for the cars people own,45 43 with more than 200 supervised test vehicles now on public highways in California and Michigan.45 42 40

Our work with kids in STEM

  • A World In Motion brings about 2,000 GM employees into K–12 classrooms for hands-on, team-based STEM activities.48 49
  • GM backed Girls Who Code with a $250,000 grant to open computer science to middle- and high-school girls from underserved communities.48 50
  • GM supplies Chevrolet Bolt EVs for the AutoDrive Challenge, where university teams build a full autonomous passenger vehicle.48 49
  • Through GM Cares, employees fund classroom projects on DonorsChoose, and GM has partnered with Disney Imagination Campus to support teachers.51 52
  • GM de México has supported FIRST Robotics for 20 years, importing fields and kits and sending GM mentors to every team.53 54

Why an AI architect cares about a fourth-grade robot

The Ridge Robotics color sensor that told water from electrolytes is perception. The run that squares against a wall before every mission is localization. The notebook of what broke and what changed is validation. Those are the three jobs of a self-driving stack. The kids are already doing the work; they just call it the Robot Game.

Super Cruise is a hands-free driver assistance technology, not a self-driving system; drivers must stay attentive. Eyes-off capability is planned for 2028 subject to development, validation and other factors.41 47 Views on this page are those of the volunteers, not official statements of General Motors.

Privacy and protecting kids

What this site does, and does not do, with information

This is a volunteer page about an elementary-school team, so it is built to collect nothing and to say as little about children as the story needs. Here is the full accounting.

Nothing is collected

  • No cookies, no analytics, no trackers, no ads. The page is static files served by the host; there is no database and no server code written by us.
  • No third-party requests. Fonts, images and scripts are served from this site. A Content Security Policy blocks anything else from loading.
  • The pledge form never leaves your device until you choose to copy it, download it, or open it in your own mail app addressed to the school office. We never see it.
  • The share and QR features point at this address only.

About the students

  • First names only, supplied by the head coach, never surnames, grades, ages, photos, or schedules.
  • Avatars are code-drawn robots, not likenesses, and they are assigned by list position, not by anything about the child.
  • Last year's team appears only as first names already published by local news and the school district, with those sources cited.
  • Removal on request. Any parent or guardian can ask the school office to have a name removed and it comes off at the next version, with the change recorded in the HIBT ledger.
  • No direct contact with students. Every contact path on this page goes to adults at the school office, consistent with the FIRST Youth Protection Program.63 64

The rules we measured against

  • FERPA. Student names can be shared as "directory information" only when the district has designated them so and families have had the chance to opt out; Ephrata publishes its FERPA notice. Because this page is not the school, we go further and rely on coach-supplied first names with family permission.60 61
  • Washington's Student User Privacy in Education Rights Act (RCW 28A.604) binds school service providers; this page is not one, but it follows the same limits anyway: no targeted ads, no selling or profiling of student information, no collection beyond the first names shown.62 66
  • COPPA. This page is not directed to children and collects no personal information from anyone, so no parental-consent mechanism is triggered; we still avoid anything a child could submit.65
  • FIRST YPP. Adults coordinate through the school; the site never asks a student for anything.63 64

Coach's checklist before adding or changing a student name

  1. Confirm the family's district media/directory permission is on file and not opted out (the office keeps the forms).
  2. Send first names only, to Bob, from a school email address.
  3. Never send photos of students for this page; it does not use them by design.
  4. If a family asks for removal, email the office; the change ships in the next version and the ledger records it.

Accessibility: this page targets WCAG 2.1 AA. It is keyboard-navigable with visible focus, has a skip link, labels every control, keeps text at a minimum 4.5:1 contrast, honors reduced-motion settings, and works at 375 px wide and in print. Found a barrier? Tell the school office and it goes on the next version's list.

How I Built This · version control

HIBT-AIGovOps ledger v1.7

This page was built with an AI assistant, and it says so. The ledger below records every prompt that shaped it: who asked, when, which model answered, what changed, and a SHA-256 hash of every file that ships. Each entry is chained to the one before it, so the record can be re-verified in your browser against the files you are looking at right now. That is the AIGovOps idea in miniature: make the governance of AI work visible, checkable and boring.

Thanks

With gratitude to the AIGovOps Foundation and its co-founders, Bob Rapp and Ken Johnston, for their work making AI safer: turning governance into policy-as-code, verifiable evidence and human-readable receipts like this one, and bringing those tools to rural and under-served communities, including schools like Columbia Ridge.

        Past champions · FIRST LEGO League Challenge · global

        Past Champions: What can we learn?

        Ridge Robotics competes in FIRST LEGO League Challenge, the same division as every team on this page. These are the World Festival Champion’s Award podiums for the last three seasons, from Houston, with nine team profiles broken down the way judges score: robot build, software, Innovation Project design, presentation and Core Values. Read it as a playbook, not a scoreboard.

        Start with the tutorial Jump to the roster Team profiles

        Tutorial

        How a Champion’s Award is actually won

        The Champion’s Award is not “best robot.” It goes to the team ranked first in the Champion’s Rank, which combines the Robot Game score with the judges’ rubrics for Robot Design, Innovation Project and Core Values; one winner and a small set of finalists are named at each event.24 At the World Festival the field is the national and regional champions of 60-plus countries.1 2

        Step 1 · Robot Game

        Consistency beats ceiling

        Ten teams hit a perfect 545 in 2026; the tiebreaks were about repeating it.6 The Mavericks’ 100 → 355 → 535 arc shows the other half: a repair plan and a spare motor matter as much as the program.14

        Step 2 · Robot Design

        Show your engineering, not just your robot

        Judges praised Robot Rampage’s gear shifting, “pencil-point accuracy” and robust testing methods8; Brazil’s Robot Design winner logged every launch in spreadsheets and filmed runs to review attachments.20 The notebook is the evidence.

        Step 3 · Innovation Project

        Real experts, real users, real tests

        ROBOTECH interviewed archaeologists and attended the professional society’s webinars5; the Mavericks deployed their UV-C rig in Sequim Bay with national-lab scientists15; Robot Rampage’s tool holder has a provisional patent and is on real dig sites.8

        Step 4 · Core Values

        Help the team at the next table

        FSIngenium lent a motor to a rival; both finished as finalists.14 Robot Rampage ran a design forum for other teams.8 Ridge already wins Core Values awards; this is the same muscle on a bigger stage.

        Ridge’s path to this list

        Qualifier → Eastern Washington State → Houston

        In Washington, the state Champion’s Award winner advances to the World Festival; a lottery sends additional strong teams to Open Invitationals, which is how Ridge reached New Jersey in 2026.25 The only Washington team ever on this podium, the Intelligent Mavericks, is a grades 5–8 team from Richland, two hours from Ephrata.12 14

        Nine profiles · three seasons

        The winners and the finalists with the most to teach

        Each season’s winner plus the finalists with the best public documentation. Where a team has not published a detail, the card says so rather than guessing. Contacts are public team, school or organization channels only; no personal phone numbers or private emails appear on this site, consistent with our privacy rules.

        2025–26 · UNEARTHED Champion’s Award winner

        ROBOTECH

        Mollerussa (Lleida), competing as Barcelona, Spain

        Who they are
        An independent, student-led STEM team (not a school team) from the small city of Mollerussa; the team describes itself as boys and girls who develop programming and robotics projects together.4
        The challenge
        The 2025–26 UNEARTHED season asked teams to use technology to explore the past: archaeology, excavation and what artifacts tell us about people. World Festival: 160 teams from 66 countries, Houston, April 29–May 2, 2026.1 13
        Innovation Project (design)
        ARKEODENS, an automated flotation and sediment-processing system that helps archaeologists recover seeds, tiny bones, shells and charcoal from soil samples by separating material by density and size. They learned flotation is slow, manual and inconsistent, so they automated part of it and built in documentation, explicitly to assist archaeologists rather than replace them. They attended Archaeological Institute of America webinars, visited sites and museums, and interviewed university, museum and heritage experts by video call.5
        Robot build
        Robot hardware is not described in public coverage, but the result is: 5th in the world in Robot Performance at the Festival, so the robot was both fast and consistent.1
        Software
        Not publicly documented; ask the team through the channel below.
        Presentation & Core Values
        The AIA, which fielded a flood of archaeology questions from FLL teams, singled out ROBOTECH for how seriously the students engaged real practitioners.5
        Why they scored so highly
        The Champion’s Award goes to the team ranked first across all four rubrics. ROBOTECH paired a top-5 robot with an Innovation Project judged by the discipline’s own professional society as genuinely useful. Lesson for Ridge: talk to the actual experts, and let them tell you what is slow and annoying in their work.1 5
        Public contact
        Team website: robotech.cat (contact form on site). No personal numbers published.

        Sources 1 4 5

        2025–26 · UNEARTHED Champion’s Award finalist

        SCRAPS by FutureLab

        Kalamaria, Thessaloniki, Greece

        Who they are
        A team from FutureLab, an educational robotics academy founded by scientists and educators, with Aristotle University of Thessaloniki’s technology-transfer company (ACTA) as strategic partner since 2019. Greek national champions in 2026.6 7
        The challenge
        The 2025–26 UNEARTHED season asked teams to use technology to explore the past: archaeology, excavation and what artifacts tell us about people. World Festival: 160 teams from 66 countries, Houston, April 29–May 2, 2026.1 13
        Innovation Project (design)
        Public coverage describes an “innovative proposal” on the archaeology theme that earned top rubric marks, but not the specifics.6
        Robot build
        A perfect Robot Game: 545 points, which ten teams matched; SCRAPS ranked 9th worldwide on tiebreak. That is every mission, every run.6
        Software
        Not publicly documented; ask the team through the channel below.
        Presentation & Core Values
        Top rubric evaluations in Robot Design, Innovation Project and Core Values, per the academy.6
        Why they scored so highly
        Balance. A maximum robot score plus top marks on all three judged rubrics is exactly the Champion’s Award formula. Lesson for Ridge: the robot ceiling is reachable, but the award is decided in the judging room.1 6
        Public contact
        Academy website: roboticsacademy.edu.gr · generic email info [at] futurelab.edu.gr (organization inbox).

        Sources 1 6 7

        2025–26 · UNEARTHED Champion’s Award finalist

        Robot Rampage

        West St. Paul, Minnesota, USA

        Who they are
        A five-student middle-school team from St. Croix Lutheran Academy, in its ninth year as a program; the current team credits earlier members for the foundation.8 9
        The challenge
        The 2025–26 UNEARTHED season asked teams to use technology to explore the past: archaeology, excavation and what artifacts tell us about people. World Festival: 160 teams from 66 countries, Houston, April 29–May 2, 2026.1 13
        Innovation Project (design)
        Tripodamus, a tool-holding invention that keeps archaeologists from losing tools and straining their backs. It has a provisional patent and is in use at active dig sites.8
        Robot build
        Judges praised shifting gears, “pencil-point accuracy” and innovative attachments. After technical trouble in two rounds, the team made fixes over the midday break and hit a team-record 500 on the final run.8
        Software
        Not publicly documented; ask the team through the channel below.
        Presentation & Core Values
        Ran a design forum to share robot methods with other teams; judges also noted robust testing methods and how the team honored absent teammates. 1st in Core Values at state.8
        Why they scored so highly
        Outreach that helps rivals, a project with real users, and the composure to repair and re-run under pressure. Lesson for Ridge: build a repair plan into competition day, and share what you know.1 8
        Public contact
        School: stcroixlutheran.org/msrobot · team site robot-rampage.com.

        2024–25 · SUBMERGED Champion’s Award winner

        SESI HEROES

        Jundiaí, São Paulo, Brazil

        Who they are
        Students of Escola SESI Jundiaí, part of the SESI-SP industry-run school network, which with this win became a three-time World Festival champion.10 11
        The challenge
        The 2024–25 SUBMERGED season asked teams to solve problems ocean explorers face, from sensors to habitats. World Festival: 160 Challenge teams, Houston, April 16–19, 2025.2 10
        Innovation Project (design)
        SmartReef, an automated extractor for removing invasive corals from the seabed, replacing divers’ mallet-and-chisel work that is slow and risky. Invasive coral is a documented problem on the São Paulo coast.10 11
        Robot build
        Not publicly documented; ask the team through the channel below.
        Software
        Not publicly documented; ask the team through the channel below.
        Presentation & Core Values
        Judges cited “exemplary performance in all evaluated categories”; the school highlights teamwork, research and programming.10
        Why they scored so highly
        A clearly scoped, locally grounded problem with a mechanical solution the team could demonstrate. Lesson for Ridge: pick a problem you can see from your own shoreline (or orchard), and show the device working.2 10

        School network: jundiai.sesisp.org.br · SESI-SP general line (11) 4210-4455 (organization, not a person).

        2024–25 · SUBMERGED Champion’s Award finalist

        Intelligent Mavericks

        Richland, Washington, USA

        Who they are
        A grades 5–8 team drawing from Lewis and Clark Elementary, Libby and Enterprise Middle Schools and Three Rivers HomeLink in the Richland School District. The first Washington team ever to reach the Champion’s finalist tier, and the only U.S. team to do so in 2025.12 14
        The challenge
        The 2024–25 SUBMERGED season asked teams to solve problems ocean explorers face, from sensors to habitats. World Festival: 160 Challenge teams, Houston, April 16–19, 2025.2 10
        Innovation Project (design)
        EPIC (Epibiosis Preventative Illuminated Contraption), an underwater UV-C lighting rig to stop biofouling on ocean sensors. Built with Pacific Northwest National Laboratory scientists, deployed twice in salt water at PNNL-Sequim and John Wayne Marina, then revised into EPIC Twist after expert feedback. Perfect Innovation Project rubric score.12 15
        Robot build
        A motor failed in match one (100 points). FSIngenium of Spain lent a spare; the team rebuilt and re-tuned, scoring 355 then 535, ten points from their maximum.14
        Software
        Reprogrammed mission paths to the replacement motor’s behavior between matches; language and tools not stated.14
        Presentation & Core Values
        Judges praised confidence, creativity and deep understanding of the science; the team shared its robot and project with attendees.14 15
        Why they scored so highly
        Real field data from a national lab partnership, plus grace under failure. Lesson for Ridge: PNNL is in Washington; so are WSU Extension, fisheries biologists and orchardists. Ask them. And carry a spare motor.2 14

        District: rsd.edu · info [at] rsd.edu · (509) 967-6000 · team site 46665robotics.weebly.com.

        Los Atômicos

        Araras, São Paulo, Brazil

        Who they are
        Escola SESI-SP de Araras (CE 303); the program dates to 2012 and the coach credits that legacy. Regional runner-up, national champion, then world champion in one season.18 19

        The 2023–24 MASTERPIECE season asked teams to explore the role STEM plays in the arts and how people share their passions. World Festival: 152 Challenge teams, Houston, April 17–20, 2024.3 16

        Built “to optimize mission time”: SPIKE kit, two large and two medium motors, two color sensors, a gyro, and a pneumatic piston kit for attachments.20

        Coach: a team of students “with values who respect each other’s opinions,” and a decade of accumulated know-how passed down.18

        Everything, consistently: the award text itself says excellence across Robot Performance, Robot Design, Innovation Project and Core Values. Lesson for Ridge: keep the notebook and the attachments from year to year; legacy is a competitive advantage.3 20

        Escola SESI de Referência de Itajaí (SESI SC network); members aged 9–15. Won Brazil’s national stage in São Paulo to qualify.22 23
        The challenge
        The 2025–26 UNEARTHED season asked teams to use technology to explore the past: archaeology, excavation and what artifacts tell us about people. World Festival: 160 teams from 66 countries, Houston, April 29–May 2, 2026.1 13
        Innovation Project (design)
        Specifics not published; the school says preparation focused on “technical improvement of the robot and developing its judged presentations.”22
        Robot build
        Not publicly documented; ask the team through the channel below.
        Software
        Not publicly documented; ask the team through the channel below.
        Presentation & Core Values
        Coach credits dedication, effort, persistence and learning; the state industry federation received the team afterward.22 23
        Why they scored so highly
        Among the five finalists out of 160 teams from 66 countries. Lesson for Ridge: practice the judged presentations as hard as the robot; this team says that is literally what they did.1 22
        Public contact
        School network: fiesc.com.br · FIESC line (48) 3231-4100 (organization).
